prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

text:
When you run git commit, you create a small set of files inside the .git directory, and understanding them explains most of Git's behavior. Everything Git stores lives in a content-addressable object database under .git/objects. Each object is identified by a SHA-1 hash (newer repositories can use SHA-256) computed from the object's type, its size and its content. That hash is the object's name, and it is also where the object lives on disk: the first two hex characters become a directory and the remaining characters become the filename, so an object with hash ab12cd... sits at .git/objects/ab/12cd.... The content is compressed with zlib, and objects are immutable. Because the name is derived from the content, two identical pieces of content always share one object, and any change to the content produces a different name.

The simplest object is the blob. A blob holds the raw bytes of a file and nothing else. It does not record the filename, the permissions or the directory the file came from. If you have two files with identical contents in different folders, or the same file in a hundred commits, Git stores a single blob for all of them. When you run git add, Git reads the file, writes a blob into the object database straight away, and records the result in the index. That is why files you have staged but never committed are already safely stored inside .git.

Names and structure belong to the tree object. A tree represents one directory, and it is a list of entries. Each entry has a file mode (for example 100644 for a regular file, 100755 for an executable, 040000 for a subdirectory, 120000 for a symlink), a name, and the hash of what it points to. For a file the target is a blob, and for a subdirectory the target is another tree. A project therefore becomes a nested structure: a root tree points to blobs for the top-level files and to trees for each subfolder, which in turn point to more blobs and trees. The hash of a tree depends on the hashes of everything beneath it, so a change to one file deep in the project changes its blob, then every tree above it up to the root. Unchanged directories keep the same hash and are reused, so a new snapshot only costs the objects that actually changed. The root tree hash is effectively a fingerprint of your entire working tree at a moment in time. You can inspect any of these with git cat-file -p followed by a hash, which prints a tree's entries or a blob's contents, and git cat-file -t prints the type.

The commit object ties a snapshot to history. It is a short text record with a handful of fields. The first is the hash of the root tree, which is the snapshot itself. Next come zero or more parent lines, giving the hashes of the commits that came directly before. An ordinary commit has one parent, the very first commit has none, and a merge commit has two or more. Then there are author and committer lines, each with a name, an email address, a timestamp and a timezone offset, and finally a blank line followed by the commit message. Note that a commit does not store a diff. Git stores complete snapshots and works out differences by comparing trees when you ask for them. Because the parent hashes are part of the commit's content, every commit's hash depends on the whole history behind it. This is why rewriting an old commit, through a rebase or an amend, creates new hashes for that commit and every descendant: the old ones are not edited, they are simply replaced by new objects. Together the commits form a directed acyclic graph, which is the history you see in git log.

All of those objects are identified by long hashes, which are impractical to work with by hand. Refs solve that by giving human-friendly names to hashes. A ref is just a file containing a commit hash. Branches live under .git/refs/heads, so the file .git/refs/heads/main holds the hash of the latest commit on main. Tags live under .git/refs/tags, and remote-tracking branches such as origin/main live under .git/refs/remotes. A branch in Git is nothing more than this tiny movable pointer, which is why creating one is instantaneous. When you commit, Git writes the new objects, creates the commit with the current commit as its parent, and then overwrites the current branch's file with the new commit's hash. The branch moves forward while all the older objects stay exactly where they were. Large repositories often pack refs into a single .git/packed-refs file for efficiency, but the idea is the same.

One more file ties the picture together. HEAD, at .git/HEAD, tells Git what you currently have checked out. Normally it is a symbolic ref, a file containing something like ref: refs/heads/main, meaning you are on that branch and new commits will advance it. If you check out a specific commit directly, HEAD instead holds a raw hash, which is the detached HEAD state.

Finally, over time Git compacts its loose objects into packfiles under .git/objects/pack, storing similar objects as deltas against each other to save space, but this is an optimization and does not change the model. Every commit is a hash-named text record pointing to a tree and to its parents, trees point to blobs and other trees, and refs are named pointers into that graph.
